strengths: LESV addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: efficient open-vocabulary querying of reconstructed 3D scenes. Combining sparse voxel geometry, confidence-weighted feature fusion, and dense language-aligned features produces a coherent, practically motivated pipeline.

The reported ScanNet improvements are substantial: 19-class mIoU increases from 31.66 for Dr. Splat to 53.22, with gains also observed for the 15- and 10-class settings. LERF average 3D retrieval improves from 52.67 to 56.11 mIoU and from 76.91 to 85.21 Acc@25.

Qualitative examples illustrate useful part-level querying and cleaner semantic boundaries. Evaluation across 3D retrieval, 2D retrieval, and point-cloud segmentation demonstrates versatility beyond a single output modality.
The manuscript includes component ablations, an alternative upsampler comparison, and supplementary mesh-fusion pseudocode. The reported three-minute feature-lifting stage suggests practical value.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the central geometric contribution from the stronger feature extractor. There is no comparison using identical RADIO/RADSeg features on Gaussian and voxel representations, or against a simple depth-based fusion baseline. In Table 4, confidence weighting adds only 0.05 mIoU, while the largest final improvement comes from the borrowed SCRA/SCGA modules. Removing geometric components from the complete pipeline and evaluating those ablations on ScanNet would better establish the source of the gains.

Evaluation details are insufficient to verify the results. Section 4.2 introduces 'normalized cosine similarity' for all methods without defining the normalization, thresholds, or their selection procedure. The ScanNet scene count, split, class subsets, and text prompts are unspecified. Its transfer protocol also uses different neighborhood sizes for Gaussians and voxels without sensitivity analysis. These omissions matter especially because the strongest result is on ScanNet.

Implementation details leave substantial reproducibility gaps: the exact RADIO checkpoint and language head, monocular prior models, loss weights, optimization schedule, voxel settings, fusion bandwidths, and sliding-window parameters are not supplied. The text alternates between AM-RADIO, RADIO-v3, SigLIP, and SigLIP-2. The supplement does not fully specify how the density representation generates the initial TSDF fields and confidence weights.

The scalability argument overstates what the formulation establishes. Gaussian registration can also be deterministic; disjoint voxels alone do not guarantee correct visibility or eliminate semantic mixing. The claimed O(1) memory applies at most to fixed-batch working memory, not the stored scene and feature field. No measured peak-memory or scene-size scaling experiments substantiate the broader claim. Table 5 also gives approximately 32 minutes total for LESV versus 30 for Dr. Splat under its stated accounting, so faster fusion should be distinguished from total pipeline speed.

The broad state-of-the-art claims exceed the comparisons. Table 2 reports lower average 2D retrieval mIoU than LangSplatV2 (56.84 versus 59.88), and slightly lower localization accuracy than LangSplat. ProFuse is discussed but omitted from quantitative evaluation, while the ScanNet comparison covers only a narrow set of Gaussian methods. LERF improvements are uneven, with lower mIoU than Dr. Splat on two of four scenes.

Originality is primarily in integrating existing components, which can be valuable, but the current controls do not establish the added value of the proposed combination convincingly enough. Claims that multi-level ambiguity is resolved rely largely on aggregate retrieval scores and selected examples, without a dedicated part-to-whole evaluation. Minor reporting issues—including Dr. Splat's inconsistent LERF average in Tables 1 and 7 and an unresolved figure reference—also require correction, although these are secondary to the evidence gaps.

strengths: LESV addresses a relevant problem: efficient, spatially precise open-vocabulary querying of reconstructed 3D scenes. Combining sparse voxel geometry, confidence-weighted feature fusion, and dense language-aligned features is a coherent approach with practical potential.

The reported quantitative improvements are meaningful. On ScanNet, Table 3 reports 53.22% mIoU versus 31.66% for Dr. Splat in the 19-class setting, with substantial gains in the other class configurations. On LERF, Table 1 improves average 3D retrieval mIoU from 52.67% to 56.11% and Acc@25 from 76.91% to 85.21%.

The paper includes component ablations, an alternative upsampling comparison, and qualitative examples of object-part retrieval and reduced spatial spillover. Table 5 also shows promising reductions in feature-lifting time, while the supplementary material provides additional mesh-extraction details and outdoor demonstrations.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the proposed geometric contribution from the stronger feature pipeline. LESV changes the representation, feature backbone, attention refinement, and fusion procedure simultaneously. A matched-feature comparison between Gaussian and voxel registration is particularly important to support the central explanation that structured geometry drives the gains. Table 4 is only sequential: depth confidence adds just 0.05 mIoU, while the largest final improvement comes from the explicitly borrowed SCRA/SCGA modules. There is no corresponding ScanNet ablation explaining the much larger gains there.

Evaluation details are insufficient to establish reproducibility and comparison fairness. Section 4.2 introduces 'normalized cosine similarity' for all methods without defining the normalization, threshold, or threshold-selection procedure. Section 4.3 changes feature transfer, using 64 Gaussian neighbors versus eight voxel neighbors and removing Mahalanobis gating, without a sensitivity study. The ScanNet scene count and split are not specified. These omissions matter because thresholding and feature transfer directly determine the reported masks and segmentation scores.

Implementation details omit essential information, including the exact RADIO checkpoint and language head, monocular-prior models, geometry-training schedule and loss weights, fusion bandwidths, crop size and stride, and TSDF settings. References to AM-RADIO, Radio-v3, SigLIP, and SigLIP-2 leave the actual feature configuration ambiguous. Describing the GPU only as equivalent to an RTX 5090 also limits reproducibility of the timing results.

The broad state-of-the-art claims exceed the evidence. Table 2 reports lower average 2D retrieval mIoU than LangSplatV2 (56.84% versus 59.88%), and localization accuracy is essentially tied with LangSplatV2 and slightly below LangSplat. In 3D retrieval, LESV loses to Dr. Splat on two of four scenes. ProFuse is discussed as a closely related registration method but is not evaluated quantitatively, and the ScanNet comparison does not establish superiority beyond the selected Gaussian-based methods. These results remain valuable, but support narrower claims.

The efficiency and scalability arguments need qualification. Table 5 supports faster feature lifting, but its listed stages total approximately 32 minutes for LESV versus 30 minutes for Dr. Splat when the latter's preprocessing dash is treated as no per-scene cost. The claimed O(1) memory can describe fixed-size fusion batches, not total scene storage, which grows with the number of voxel features. No measured peak-memory or scene-scaling experiment substantiates the broader claim. Likewise, non-overlapping voxels do not inherently eliminate visibility uncertainty or incorrect feature mixing; deterministic computation alone does not establish semantic correctness.

Several reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence in the presentation: Dr. Splat's average 3D mIoU is 52.67% in Table 1 but 53.67% in supplementary Table 7, and the prose describing ramen results disagrees with Table 2. These are individually correctable. The main reason for weak rejection is the more consequential combination of under-specified evaluation and insufficient controlled evidence for the claimed geometric mechanism.

strengths: LESV addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: efficient, fine-grained language querying directly in 3D. Combining sparse voxel geometry, geometry-aware feature fusion, and dense language-aligned features is a coherent design with practical value.

The reported 3D results are promising. On LERF, LESV improves average mIoU from 52.67% to 56.11% and Acc@25 from 76.91% to 85.21% over Dr. Splat. ScanNet improvements are particularly substantial: 53.22% versus 31.66% mIoU for 19 classes, with gains also reported for 15 and 10 classes.

The qualitative examples illustrate useful capabilities, including small-object retrieval, part-level queries, and reduced spillover. The supplementary upsampling comparison and sequential ablations provide evidence that feature processing and geometric regularization contribute to performance.

The pipeline offers meaningful efficiency advantages over the evaluated distillation methods. Table 5 reports approximately 3 minutes for feature lifting and 14 minutes for preprocessing, compared with 60 and 120 minutes for LangSplat, respectively.
weaknesses: Evaluation details are insufficient to establish reproducibility and comparison fairness. Section 4.2 introduces normalized cosine similarity for all methods without specifying the normalization, thresholds, or how these were selected. ScanNet scene counts, scene identities, and evaluation split are unspecified. Section 4.3 also changes feature transfer and uses different neighborhoods for Gaussians and voxels without a sensitivity analysis. These omissions materially limit confidence in the reported gains.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the central representation claim from the stronger feature extractor. There is no comparison using the same RADIO features and refinement modules on Gaussian and voxel backbones. SCRA and SCGA are adopted from RADSeg and provide the largest final ablation improvement, whereas depth confidence adds only 0.05 mIoU points in Table 4. A full-model removal ablation and comparison against the directly relevant ProFuse method would better establish the contribution of the proposed fusion mechanism.

Important implementation choices remain unspecified: the exact RADIO checkpoint and language head, monocular depth/normal estimators, loss weights, fusion bandwidths, crop configuration, and TSDF fusion settings. The manuscript alternates between AM-RADIO, RADIO-v3, and SigLIP-2 terminology. Algorithm 1 also leaves TSDF construction largely abstract. Together, these gaps make faithful reconstruction difficult.

The scalability argument is overstated. Disjoint voxels do not by themselves eliminate visibility uncertainty, and Gaussian registration can also be deterministic. Batching can bound working memory, but the voxel feature field still scales with scene size; the claimed O(1) memory therefore needs a precise accounting. No peak-memory or scene-size scaling measurements substantiate this claim. Moreover, Table 5 totals approximately 32 minutes for LESV versus 30 minutes for Dr. Splat, so faster feature lifting does not demonstrate faster end-to-end processing against that baseline.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Table 2 does not support state-of-the-art average 2D retrieval: LESV obtains 56.84% mIoU versus LangSplatV2's 59.88%, and its localization accuracy is slightly below LangSplat's. LESV also trails Dr. Splat in 3D mIoU on two of four LERF scenes. Qualitative part queries and KITTI-360 examples support feasibility, but do not establish that semantic ambiguity is resolved or that the method is ready for downstream autonomous planning. These claims should be narrowed; the more consequential acceptance concerns are the evaluation and attribution gaps above.

strengths: LESV addresses a relevant computer-vision problem with a coherent integration of sparse voxel geometry, confidence-weighted feature fusion, and dense language-aligned features. Avoiding hierarchical mask extraction while supporting direct 3D queries has practical value.

The reported ScanNet improvements are substantial: 53.22% versus 31.66% mIoU for Dr. Splat on 19 classes, and 30.65% versus 17.88% on ScanNet200. LERF results also support competitive retrieval, with 56.11% mIoU and the highest reported Acc@25 of 85.21%.

Evaluation covers 3D retrieval, projected 2D retrieval, and point-cloud segmentation. Qualitative examples show cleaner object boundaries and useful part-level localization; the supplementary outdoor examples suggest additional applications.

The paper provides component ablations and an informative comparison of feature upsampling strategies. It appropriately credits inherited methods, including SVRaster and RADSeg, and explicitly discusses resolution limitations and the lack of real-time feature rendering.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is insufficiently isolated. Table 5 compares mask-pooled AM-RADIO features for Dr. Splat against dense AM-RADIO features with additional processing for LESV, changing more than the representation. With matched SAM+CLIP features, Table 4 shows only a 0.40-point ScanNet mIoU advantage, while LERF Acc@25 decreases. A baseline registering identical processed dense features onto another representation, and ablations of geometric components under the final dense-feature configuration, are needed to establish what drives the gains.

The claimed fundamental scalability advantage is overstated. Spatial batching can bound working memory, but storing voxel geometry and high-dimensional features still scales with scene size unless explicitly streamed. Gaussian registration is also deterministic given its weights, and the manuscript does not establish that dense registration onto Gaussians is intrinsically infeasible. Table 6 measures four scenes without separating host memory, GPU memory, and output storage or providing a controlled scaling experiment.

Reproducibility is substantially limited. The manuscript omits the ScanNet scene count and split, exact RADIO checkpoint and language head, monocular prior models, optimization schedule and loss weights, fusion bandwidths, crop configuration, and TSDF hyperparameters. The normalized cosine-similarity transformation, retrieval thresholds, and their selection protocol are particularly important because the reported retrieval metrics depend directly on them.

The broad state-of-the-art claim exceeds the comparison coverage. ScanNet evaluation primarily compares against Gaussian language-field methods, while the closely discussed ProFuse is absent from quantitative comparisons. OpenVoxel appears only in the supplementary comparison. The evidence supports strong results against the evaluated baselines, but does not establish leadership across open-vocabulary point-cloud understanding generally.

The efficiency reporting needs consistent accounting. Table 7 totals approximately 32 minutes for LESV, whereas the text elsewhere cites approximately 20 minutes; its approximately 85% reduction relative to the listed LaGa total does not substantiate the claimed 90% reduction in total processing time. Baseline feature-extraction costs, monocular-prior computation, and precise hardware should be accounted for consistently.

As an Algorithms/General submission, the integration is promising, but most components are inherited and the distinctive fusion contribution has limited isolated quantitative support. Together with the evaluation and reproducibility gaps, this leaves a slight preference for rejection despite the encouraging overall results.

strengths: LESV addresses a relevant computer vision problem: efficient, open-vocabulary querying of reconstructed 3D scenes. Combining sparse voxels, geometry-aware feature fusion, and dense language-aligned features is a coherent and potentially useful design.

The reported segmentation improvements are substantial. ScanNet-19 mIoU increases from 31.66 for Dr. Splat to 53.22, and the supplementary ScanNet200 experiment reports 30.65 versus 17.88. LERF results also demonstrate competitive retrieval, including the highest reported Acc@25 of 85.21.

The paper includes useful component studies: geometry ablations with fixed SAM+CLIP features, representation/backbone comparisons, and supplementary upsampling experiments. Qualitative examples illustrate reduced spillover and successful part-level queries.

The manuscript credits its major inherited components, including SVRaster, AM-RADIO, and RADSeg. Its discussion of limited feature resolution and lack of real-time feature rendering usefully qualifies practical applicability.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not established by the ablations. Table 5 compares mask-pooled AM-RADIO features for Dr. Splat against dense, spatially processed features for LESV, changing feature granularity and processing alongside representation. It therefore does not isolate the advantage of sparse voxels over Gaussian geometry. With identical SAM+CLIP features, the ScanNet improvement is only 0.40 mIoU, while LERF Acc@25 decreases from 76.91 to 72.91. A baseline using the same dense features and comparable geometric projection or streaming registration is needed to substantiate the stronger architectural conclusions.

Evaluation and implementation details are insufficient for reproducing the main results. The paper does not specify the ScanNet evaluation scene count or split, the exact normalized-cosine transformation and retrieval thresholds, or their selection procedure. Important implementation choices are also missing, including the precise RADIO checkpoint and language head, monocular-prior model, geometry-loss weights, fusion bandwidths, and sliding-window configuration. References to AM-RADIO, RADIO-v3, CLIP, and SigLIP-2 do not clearly identify the actual feature pipeline.

The state-of-the-art claim for open-vocabulary point-cloud understanding is broader than the comparisons support. Table 3 predominantly compares Gaussian-based methods; ProFuse is discussed and supplies the transfer protocol but is not evaluated. OpenVoxel appears only in the supplement, without establishing equivalent evaluation conditions. The altered Gaussian feature-transfer procedure also lacks a sensitivity analysis. These omissions matter because the strongest quantitative evidence comes from this task.

The explanation of deterministic fusion and scalability overstates what follows from the representation. Gaussian rendering and registration can also be deterministic; disjoint voxels do not by themselves eliminate depth uncertainty or occlusion errors. Spatial batching can bound temporary feature-fusion memory, but the claimed O(1) memory regardless of scene scale does not account for geometry, accumulated voxel features, or image features unless an explicit streaming/storage model is specified. Four LERF scenes do not establish the asserted asymptotic limitation of Gaussian methods or scene-independent memory for LESV.

Efficiency comparisons need clearer accounting. Table 6 does not distinguish host RAM from GPU memory or fully specify what is resident at peak usage. Table 7 excludes Dr. Splat preprocessing through its pretrained codebook while reporting LESV feature extraction, so the totals have different accounting boundaries. Including the listed stages gives approximately 32 minutes for LESV versus 30 for Dr. Splat; the practical advantage is therefore primarily over slower mask-based pipelines, rather than a universal end-to-end speed advantage.

Under the default Algorithms/General category, originality lies mainly in integrating established components, making controlled evidence especially important. The supplement shows that sliding-window aggregation alone reduces LERF mIoU from 51.19 to 49.79, whereas adding inherited RADSeg modules raises it to 56.11. This deserves clearer attribution in the explanation of the gains. Together with the confounded representation comparison and incomplete evaluation specification, the current evidence leaves important concerns that outweigh the promising reported performance.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General, LESV presents a useful integration of sparse voxel geometry, confidence-weighted feature fusion, and dense language-aligned features. The practical contribution is a coherent pipeline for direct 3D querying without hierarchical mask preprocessing.

The reported ScanNet gains are substantial: 53.22% versus 31.66% mIoU for Dr. Splat on 19 classes, with improvements across the 15-, 10-, and 200-class evaluations. These results support the value of the complete pipeline.

LERF results demonstrate competitive retrieval across modalities: LESV achieves 56.11% 3D mIoU and the highest reported Acc@25 of 85.21%. Its 2D localization accuracy is comparable to LangSplatV2 despite using direct feature registration.

The ablations provide useful evidence beyond aggregate performance. Table 4 evaluates geometric refinement under shared SAM+CLIP features, while Table 8 shows that the adopted SCRA/SCGA aggregation improves over raw features and simple sliding-window aggregation. The discussion candidly identifies resolution and feature-rendering limitations.

The reported reduction in preprocessing and feature-lifting time is practically attractive. Overall, the substantial empirical gains and useful integration support a slight preference for acceptance, although the attribution and reproducibility concerns below prevent a stronger recommendation.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not fully isolated. Table 5 compares mask-pooled AM-RADIO features in Dr. Splat against dense features in LESV, changing both representation and feature aggregation. With identical SAM+CLIP features, the ScanNet advantage is only 0.40 mIoU. A baseline that projects the same dense features onto Gaussians, points, or a conventional voxel reconstruction would better establish which gains require the proposed geometry and fusion.

Reproducibility is insufficiently specified. The manuscript does not clearly identify the evaluated ScanNet scene count and split, exact RADIO checkpoint and language head, monocular prior models, loss weights, fusion bandwidths, crop settings, or similarity-normalization and threshold-selection procedures. These omissions matter because the evaluation modifies both feature transfer and relevance scoring relative to existing methods.

The scalability argument overstates what is demonstrated. Spatial batching can bound working memory, but storing per-voxel embeddings still scales with scene size unless an explicit streaming or external-storage scheme is provided. Four LERF scenes do not establish scene-independent total memory. Likewise, implementation-specific proposal caching does not establish that dense Gaussian registration is inherently infeasible; the claimed deterministic-versus-probabilistic distinction needs more precise formulation.

The novelty is primarily in integration: SVRaster, monocular geometric losses, dense agglomerative features, and SCRA/SCGA come from prior work. The distinctive confidence gating and multi-level TSDF fusion deserve stronger isolated evaluation, particularly with the final dense-feature configuration. Current evidence does not show how much these components contribute to the headline gains.

Several claims and numerical summaries need correction or qualification. LESV does not lead overall 2D retrieval mIoU, and multi-level LaGa leads 3D mIoU. Table 7 totals approximately 32 minutes for LESV, inconsistent with the approximately 20-minute comparison in the text. Dr. Splat's LERF average also varies across Tables 1, 4, and 9. These are correctable issues, but the broad state-of-the-art and efficiency statements should match the reported measurements.
